title: The text itself
hook: scholars also test whether the text fits the Qur'an and known sunnah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the isnad, the chain, and your line: who told whom. When you passed on news, did you say where it came from? Today, the other half of every hadith. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

Aisha has just heard a report that troubles her. It came through people she respects: Umar, and his son Abdullah. The report says a dead person is punished because their family weeps over them. Someone in the grave, punished for a grieving mother's tears? Aisha doesn't attack the men who carried it. She goes to the words themselves, and to the Qur'an. Her answer, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, shows a hadith's text being weighed, not just its chain. Today, the matn.
screen: `A REPORT THAT TROUBLES HER.` → `NOT THE MEN, THE WORDS.` → `WEIGHED AGAINST THE QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Matn is the text of a hadith, the part after the names: what was actually said or done. Yesterday's chain asks who carried it. The matn asks: does this fit? Second, Aisha's test. In Bukhari, she says, in effect: may Allah have mercy on Umar, but the Prophet ﷺ didn't say that about a believer. He said it about a man who rejected faith, whose punishment was being increased while his family wept. And then she reaches for the Qur'an: enough for you is the Book, which says no soul carries another's load. In the version in Sahih Muslim she adds something gentle. The men who reported it weren't liars, she says. But hearing can slip. That's the whole idea in one breath. An honest chain can still carry a misheard sentence, so the words get tested on their own. Third, what later scholars did with it. They didn't simply throw one report away. They asked how the reports fit together. Al-Bukhari's own chapter heading reads the saying narrowly: it applies, he suggests, when wailing had been the dead person's own custom. Others reconciled it in other ways. Fourth, the questions a careful reader asks of any text. Does it clash with the Qur'an? With sunnah that's well established? Does it promise a mountain of reward for a tiny act, or speak in a way that doesn't sound like him at all? Later scholars, such as Ibn al-Qayyim, gathered signs like these in their books. The chain gets a report through the door. The text still has to sit at the table with everything else that's known.
screen: `MATN: THE WORDS THEMSELVES.` · `AISHA REACHES FOR THE QUR'AN.` · `HOW DO THE REPORTS FIT?` · `QUESTIONS FOR ANY TEXT.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a text critically. Settle, and breathe. Find a quote you've seen recently with a famous name on it. A line on a poster, a caption, something forwarded with a picture of a scholar or a saint or a president. Set the name aside for a moment and look only at the words. Does it sound like the rest of what that person said? Does it promise too much? Does it clash with something you know they stood for? You don't need a verdict. Just ask the questions Aisha asked, slowly, of one sentence. The bell holds the time.
Matn. The text of a hadith, what was said or done, tested on its own against the Qur'an and the known sunnah. Today's word.
Your line: the words are tested too. Today, before you repeat a quote, read it once without the name attached. Tomorrow: sound, good, weak. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Hadith scholars examine a report's text as well as its chain, asking whether it agrees with the Qur'an, with well-established sunnah and with other reports, and they discuss how apparently conflicting reports fit together.
